meta.theme: why satire fails against a figure who cannot be shamed: its force is borrowed from what the target has staked on an audience's good opinion, and what survives is an audience-facing function the author refuses to call equivalent

meta.reviewer_notes: A narrative that looks like an anecdote about a spoiled joke and is really about where a joke's force comes from. The set punishes the two easy readings: that the sketch was at fault, and that the closing paragraph is a consolation.

quality.adversarial_review: Three accounts of why the sketch cost the minister nothing now compete across all four questions, and the passage decides between them twice. The first rival locates the failure in the channel: the target took possession of the clip, so an attack reaching its audience through his own hands arrives as a testimonial. It holds an option in every question (Q1 'turned into something other than an attack', Q2 'cannot control the terms', Q3 'convert an attack into publicity', Q4 the endorsement strengthener) and dies on 'It was borrowed, all of it, from what the target had staked', which puts the cause in the target's position rather than in who posted the clip; the passage's contrast is between a figure who pledged his seriousness and one who never asked, not between a sketch that was shared and one that was not. The second rival locates the failure in the audience: laughter that is passed on rather than converted into a verdict withdraws nothing. It dies on the first paragraph, where the audience does judge — the laugh 'had an edge to it, the sound an audience makes when it has been shown something it had noticed without ever naming' — and on the fourth, where the audience's confirmation of a standard is called real work rather than a failure. The third rival is the concession taken for the position, that satire's power over public men is simply gone and the shared laugh is what it is now for; the passage refuses it in terms — 'it would be a consolation to pretend that the second function is as good as the first, and it is not' — and keeps the class of vulnerable targets in the present tense. Q4's near-tie remains the option about earlier politicians, which is consistent with every account on offer and therefore supports none of them. Strength parity was imposed across the set afterwards: no distractor in this file is quantified more strongly than its key, because a single overreaching option was found to condemn the whole reading it belonged to without the passage being read.

blind_solve.notes: full agreement Options rebuilt against an explicit shadow thesis (a coherent rival reading carried across every question in the passage) so that the option sets no longer form a single consistent clique; the item awaits a re-solve. A second pass then removed the strength asymmetry two blind readers named as the residual channel: every distractor is now hedged no more strongly than its key, and where the passage itself asserts something flatly the key carries the absolute, so that the most cautious option is no longer reliably the answer. A third pass closed four key-to-key paraphrase and entailment leaks between questions, replaced the true options of the NOT item with framing rather than mechanism, and removed two distractors that hardening had made true. A fourth pass repaired two distractors that hardening had made defensible (an inference option entailed on a causal reading, and a purpose option with no false half) and removed a shape cue from the NOT item.

paragraphs.text: For a few weeks one winter I sat in on rehearsals for a topical revue, which is an unglamorous business: eight people in a cold room arguing about whether a joke has a fortnight left in it. The best thing in the show was an impression. A young performer had caught a junior minister exactly — not the voice, which anyone can do, but a particular way he had of pausing before a lie, as though consulting a document that did not exist. It was cruel and it was accurate, and on the first night the laugh it drew had an edge to it, the sound an audience makes when it has been shown something it had noticed without ever naming. By the Thursday the minister had posted the clip himself. Worth watching, he wrote. The sketch stayed in the programme for another week and then quietly left it. Nobody decided anything.

It is tempting to say the sketch had been stolen, and the company said something like that at the time. But nothing had been taken from it; what it wanted had simply not been there to take. Satire has never worked by making a target look foolish. A caricature does that, and no government has ever fallen to a caricature. It works by showing a man to the people whose good opinion he requires, in a light he would not have chosen. The performer supplies the light, the audience supplies the judgement, and the target supplies the need. Remove the third and the first two have nothing to act on.

That need is not a weakness of character but a security posted in advance. A figure who has spent years asking to be thought serious has pledged his seriousness, and ridicule can foreclose on it. A figure who never asked owns nothing the laughter can take: his standing rests on a following that reads mockery from outside as proof of the distance it elected him to keep. To such a man the clip is not an injury but a testimonial, and the better the impression, the better the testimonial. The force of satire was never in the portrait. It was borrowed, all of it, from what the target had staked.

What remains is smaller and is not nothing. An audience that laughs at a public man is doing something for itself as well as to him: it is confirming that a standard still exists and can still be applied, which is a thing a room of strangers can discover only together. Where the target cannot be shamed, that confirmation is the whole of satire's work, and the work is worth doing, since a people that loses the ability to say what is absurd loses more than a joke. But it would be a consolation to pretend that the second function is as good as the first, and it is not. The old sketch changed what a minister could afford to do. The new one changes only what we can still bear to notice.

questions.target_mistake: moving the cause from what the target staked to who circulated the clip or to what the audience did with it, or generalising one target's immunity into the end of satire's power over public men
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: since the force is borrowed from the target's stake and not from the portrait, anything done to the portrait alone leaves the outcome where it was.
questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: A portrait its target can circulate himself has been turned into something other than an attack.
options.B: Where a clip is passed on without being judged, the failure of satire lies with its audience.
options.C: Satire of the kind that once changed what a politician could afford to do has run out of targets.
options.D: Making a satirical portrait sharper or crueller would not restore its force against a target of this kind.

explanation.expert_notice: Two sentences in the third paragraph settle every option: 'the better the impression, the better the testimonial', and 'The force of satire was never in the portrait. It was borrowed, all of it, from what the target had staked.' If the force is borrowed from the stake, improving the portrait improves the thing that was never doing the work.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option follows directly from the causal claim. The passage locates satire's force outside the performance, in what the target has pledged to an audience; against a man who has pledged nothing there is nothing to draw on, and the passage adds that a better impression makes a better testimonial. So sharpening the portrait cannot restore a force that did not live there, and the option says only that, with no claim about other targets.
explanation.question_type_note: When a passage states where a phenomenon's power comes from, the inference questions test whether the reader keeps that source fixed; options that relocate the power into the most visible feature are the standard trap.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author says that the force of something is borrowed from elsewhere, treat every option that proposes to improve the visible thing as suspect. Ask what the sentence says is actually carrying the weight.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage puts the cause elsewhere and says so without qualification: 'It was borrowed, all of it, from what the target had staked.' The minister's posting of the clip is the moment the failure became visible, not the reason for it; a figure who owns nothing the laughter can take would have been untouched whoever circulated the sketch.
distractors.seductive_element: The clip's reappearance in the target's own hands is the turn of the anecdote, and what a story turns on is easily taken for what it is about.

distractors.why_wrong: The audience in this anecdote did judge. The first paragraph describes a laugh with 'an edge to it, the sound an audience makes when it has been shown something it had noticed without ever naming', and the passage locates the failure elsewhere in a sentence that admits no share: 'It was borrowed, all of it, from what the target had staked.' The fourth paragraph then credits the audience with work still being done rather than work withheld.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage gives the audience a decisive part — it 'supplies the judgement' — so a reader with that phrase in mind blames the party whose contribution the author has just named.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage keeps the vulnerable target in the present tense: a figure who 'has spent years asking to be thought serious has pledged his seriousness, and ridicule can foreclose on it'. Only the figure who never asked is immune, which is a claim about one kind of target rather than about the supply of them.
distractors.seductive_element: The closing contrast between the old sketch and the new one has the cadence of an ending, and an elegiac last paragraph invites a reader to make the loss general.

questions.target_mistake: choosing a condition drawn from the anecdote's machinery — who controlled the clip, what the audience did with it, when the politician held office — instead of the condition the third paragraph states
questions.stem: According to the passage, ridicule costs a public figure something only when that figure

options.A: has lost control of the terms on which the mockery reaches the people whose opinion he needs
options.B: has staked something on the good opinion the laughter would withdraw
options.C: is mocked before an audience large enough for the mockery to spread widely
options.D: belongs to a generation of politicians whose standing could still be injured from outside

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph gives the condition twice, in a matched pair: the man who 'has pledged his seriousness' can be foreclosed on; the man who 'never asked owns nothing the laughter can take'. A condition stated as a contrast between two cases is the sentence a detail question is built from.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option restates that pledge. The passage's word for it is a security posted in advance: damage is possible only where the target has already committed something to an audience, so that the audience's changed opinion takes something real away. The minister of the anecdote had committed nothing, which is why the clip cost him nothing.
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question about a stated condition is answered from the sentence that states it; the decoys will be other true features of the same episode that the passage never makes conditions.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage says something works 'only when', copy the clause after the 'when'. Options that substitute a vivid feature of the example for the stated condition are the commonest way to lose an easy mark.

distractors.why_wrong: Control of the channel is not the condition the passage names. The minister enlarged the clip's audience himself and was unharmed, and the account given is that a figure who never asked to be thought serious 'owns nothing the laughter can take' — a fact about what he has pledged, not about who carries the picture to whom.
distractors.seductive_element: The episode's hinge is an act of distribution, and the word 'terms' makes the option sound like a careful statement of what the anecdote shows.

distractors.why_wrong: Reach cannot be the condition here, since the minister enlarged the clip's audience himself and was unharmed by doing so. The passage locates the cost in what has been pledged — a figure who never asked to be thought serious 'owns nothing the laughter can take' — and says the better the impression, the better the testimonial, which would be false if spread were what did the damage.
distractors.seductive_element: It is what everyone assumes about mockery, and the anecdote's turning point is an act that multiplies the clip's audience, so the reader is handed the idea and then never told in so many words to drop it.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage makes the difference a difference between kinds of figure, not between periods: one who has pledged his seriousness can still be foreclosed on, while one who never asked cannot, and both descriptions are given in the present tense.
distractors.seductive_element: The final paragraph's contrast between the old sketch and the new one reads as a claim about two eras, and a reader who has taken it that way will look for the date.

questions.target_mistake: accepting the surviving function as the author's settled position, or relocating the failure into the channel or the audience when the passage locates it in what the target had staked
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the author uses one failed sketch to name the condition satire has always depended on, and then moves satire's surviving purpose from the target to the audience without calling the two equal.
questions.stem: Which of the following best characterises what the author does in the passage?

options.A: shows how a target's use of a sketch can convert an attack into publicity, and asks what satire keeps when it does
options.B: traces a sketch's failure to an audience that laughed without judging, and asks what laughter is now for
options.C: uses one failed sketch to name the condition satire depends on, then moves its remaining purpose to the audience
options.D: shows that satire has lost its power over public men and offers the pleasure of a shared laugh instead

explanation.expert_notice: The passage has two hinges. The first is 'nothing had been taken from it; what it wanted had simply not been there to take', which converts an anecdote into an analysis. The second is 'What remains is smaller and is not nothing', which shifts the beneficiary of satire from the target to the room. A characterisation must name both moves.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps the verb and the object of each move. The anecdote is not evidence that the sketch was bad — the passage insists it was cruel and accurate — but the occasion for stating a condition, that satire draws on what the target has staked. The final paragraph then relocates the purpose: the laugh confirms a standard for the people who are not the target. That relocation, not a verdict on satire in general, is where the passage ends.
explanation.question_type_note: Best-characterisation questions are answered in verbs. Name what the author does to the material, paragraph by paragraph, and reject options whose verbs the passage never performs.
explanation.reading_habit: Before the options, say the passage aloud as two or three verbs with objects: recounts an episode, names a condition, relocates a purpose. An option that adds a verb the author never used, such as blames or recommends, is out however true its nouns are.

distractors.why_wrong: The minister's use of the clip is the episode the argument starts from, not the explanation it reaches. The passage says the force 'was borrowed, all of it, from what the target had staked', and its third paragraph is spent distinguishing the figure who has pledged something from the figure who has not — a distinction that would be idle if the trouble were the way the sketch travelled.
distractors.seductive_element: The posting of the clip is the most vivid event in the piece, and a characterisation built on the vivid event sounds like a summary of it.

distractors.why_wrong: The audience is the one party the passage does not fault. Its laugh is described as carrying an edge, and the closing paragraph credits it with confirming that a standard 'still exists and can still be applied'. The question the last paragraph asks is what that confirmation is worth, not why the laughter failed.
distractors.seductive_element: The final paragraph really does turn to the audience, so an option that puts the audience at both ends of the argument looks like the shape of the piece.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage refuses exactly this reading: 'it would be a consolation to pretend that the second function is as good as the first, and it is not.' It also limits the loss to targets who have staked nothing rather than declaring satire powerless over public men in general.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the near-tie: the last paragraph does describe a surviving pleasure, and an elegiac closing cadence makes the whole passage sound like a lament.

questions.target_mistake: strengthening a rival account of the failure — the channel or the audience — or accepting a fact consistent with every account on offer as support for one of them
questions.prediction_target: The learner should first name the mechanism — damage requires dependence on an audience whose good opinion can be withdrawn — and predict that the strengthener compares figures who have that dependence with figures who do not.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's explanation of why the sketch cost the minister nothing?

options.A: Politicians who need approval from outside their own following lose standing when satirised; those who need only their following do not.
options.B: Satirical clips that reach an audience through the target's own account of them are received as endorsement rather than as attack.
options.C: Audiences that once treated a satirical portrait as a verdict on its subject now treat it mainly as entertainment to pass on.
options.D: Politicians of an earlier generation lost standing after being satirised far more often than politicians do today.

explanation.expert_notice: The explanation is causal and it names its variable: the target 'supplies the need', and where the need is absent the performance has nothing to act on. A strengthener must therefore vary the need and hold the ridicule constant.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option does exactly that. It compares two kinds of politician who are equally satirised and differ only in whether they depend on approval from outside their own following, and it reports the difference in outcome the author's account predicts. That is direct support for the mechanism rather than for the single episode, which is what the question asks about.
explanation.question_type_note: A strengthen question is about the link between evidence and conclusion. Name the variable the author says is doing the work, then choose the option that manipulates that variable and nothing else.
explanation.reading_habit: Write the author's claim as 'because X, therefore Y', and ask of each option whether it bears on X or only on Y. Options that confirm the outcome without touching the mechanism are the standard near-miss on strengthen questions.

distractors.why_wrong: This supports a different explanation, in which the damage is cancelled by who delivers the picture. The author's mechanism is what the target has staked, and on that account the clip would have been a testimonial to this minister's following however it arrived; strengthening the channel account leaves the author's account exactly where it was.
distractors.seductive_element: It concerns the very act the anecdote turns on, and it is written in the passage's own vocabulary of testimonials.

distractors.why_wrong: It strengthens the claim that the audience stopped judging, which the passage contradicts twice: the first-night laugh had an edge to it, and the closing paragraph credits the audience with confirming a standard. An explanation whose premise the passage denies cannot be made stronger by evidence for that premise.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like a diagnosis of the present moment, and the passage's last paragraph does discuss what the audience is now doing.

distractors.why_wrong: A general decline is what every account on offer predicts — the channel account, the audience account and the author's — so it discriminates between none of them. A strengthener has to make the author's mechanism likelier than its rivals, and this one is silent about mechanism.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the near-tie: it is about satire's effect on politicians, it points the right way, and it is exactly the sort of fact a reader expects to be asked to weigh.

vocabulary.passage_use: has pledged his seriousness, and ridicule can foreclose on it
vocabulary.meaning_here: to seize what was pledged as security when the pledge is broken

vocabulary.passage_use: the clip is not an injury but a testimonial
vocabulary.meaning_here: a public endorsement; evidence in the target's favour rather than against him

vocabulary.passage_use: A caricature does that, and no government has ever fallen to a caricature
vocabulary.meaning_here: an exaggerated portrait that distorts a subject for comic effect

mentor.challenge: A story about a joke that stopped working, told by someone who admires the joke. Decide early what the author thinks went wrong, because three of the obvious answers are wrong and the passage says so.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: A first-rate satirical impression cost its target nothing because satire's force is borrowed from what the target has staked on other people's good opinion, and where nothing has been staked the only thing left for satire to do is to remind an audience that it still has a standard.
mentor.main_idea: Satire does not work by making someone look foolish. It works by showing a person to the people whose good opinion he needs. A politician who needs no such opinion has nothing to lose, so ridicule becomes a compliment to his own side. What is left of satire is a service to the audience rather than a weapon against the target, and the author says plainly that this is a smaller thing.
mentor.simple_explanation:
The writer spends a few weeks watching a comedy show being rehearsed. The best part is an impression of a minister, and it is very good: not just the voice, but the way the man pauses before telling a lie. The first audience laughs the way people laugh when someone finally says out loud what they had only half noticed.

Then the minister posts the clip himself, with the words 'worth watching'. The sketch keeps going for a week and then disappears from the show.

The company felt robbed. The writer says nothing was stolen, because the thing the sketch was reaching for was never there. Satire has never worked simply by making someone look silly; a rude drawing can do that, and no government has ever fallen because of a drawing. It works when it shows a person to the people whose approval he needs, in a light he would not have chosen. Three things are needed: the performer's light, the audience's judgement, and the target's need. Take away the need and the other two have nothing to push against.

So the real question is what a politician has promised. A man who has spent years asking to be taken seriously has put his seriousness up as security, and mockery can take it. A man who never asked has put up nothing. His supporters treat mockery from outsiders as proof that he is not one of them, which is why they chose him. For him the clip is not a wound; it is a reference. And the better the impression, the better the reference.

What is left? When an audience laughs at a public figure, it is also doing something for itself: agreeing that a standard still exists and can still be used. That is worth having, and a country that cannot say what is absurd has lost more than a joke. But the writer refuses to call it a fair exchange. The old sketch changed what a minister could get away with. The new one only changes what we can still bring ourselves to notice.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage keeps praising the thing that failed, which readers find hard to hold. Because the sketch is described as cruel and accurate, the mind looks for a fault in it and the options offer several. The argument's real move is an abstraction dropped into the middle of a story: satire's force is borrowed, not produced, and the lender is the target. The closing paragraph then performs a second difficult move, granting a real value to what remains and immediately refusing to call it equivalent, so that both an optimistic and a despairing reading are available to anyone who stops one sentence early.
mentor.author_intention: To stop the reader from blaming the satirist, and to replace a vague sense that mockery has stopped working with a precise account of what mockery was ever working on.

paragraph_journey.note: A comedy company rehearses a superb impression of a minister. The minister shares the clip himself, and the sketch quietly disappears from the show.
Nothing was stolen. Satire never worked by making someone look silly; it works by showing him to people whose approval he needs. Three parts are required, and the target supplies one of them.
Damage is possible only where something has been pledged. A man who never asked to be thought serious owns nothing the laughter can take, and the better the impression, the better it serves him.
What survives is the audience's confirmation that a standard still exists, which is worth doing. The author then refuses to pretend it is as good as what was lost.

mentor.tone_progression: Warm and observational in the anecdote, cooler and more analytical as the mechanism is set out, and finally level and unconsoled, granting the smaller function its worth in one sentence and denying it equivalence in the next.
key_transitions: 'But nothing had been taken from it; what it wanted had simply not been there to take.' (paragraph 2) — the anecdote becomes an argument.
'The force of satire was never in the portrait.' (end of paragraph 3) — the claim the whole passage exists to make.
'But it would be a consolation to pretend that the second function is as good as the first, and it is not.' (paragraph 4) — the refusal that stops the ending from being comforting.
mentor.misunderstanding: Readers in a hurry build one of two wrong pictures. The first is that the sketch was somehow at fault and the passage is about how satire should be done better, which the text contradicts by praising the sketch and saying a sharper one would only serve the target more. The second is that the last paragraph is a consolation prize the author accepts, so that the passage ends in gentle optimism. The author's last three sentences exist precisely to block that, and a reader who stops at 'the work is worth doing' will misread the tone of the whole piece.
mentor.traps_summary: Two habits are punished here. One is transferring a cause: options move satire's power into the portrait, the audience or the size of the audience, when the passage has already said where it comes from. The other is dropping a limit: the failure is stated for one kind of target, and options offer it for all public figures and for satire as such. When an author says a thing works 'only when', the limit is the answer and the generalisation is the trap.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage tells a story and then explains it, find the sentence where the explanation names its cause, and treat that sentence as the passage's law. Every later question about what would help, what would change, or what follows is decided by whether the option touches that named cause or merely touches the story. Vivid details from the narrative will be offered as causes; they are only scenery unless the author says otherwise.
mentor.real_world: The same structure governs apologies, boycotts and public criticism of every kind: pressure works on people who have something posted with the public, and looks absurd when applied to people who have posted nothing.
mentor.takeaway: Mockery can only collect a debt that the target has already agreed to owe.
mentor.reflection_question: What have you staked on the good opinion of people you will never meet, and what would it cost you to be laughed at by them?
